As to the race itself: George Tyrer went off with his usual long start, with George Still going off next, and George managed to keep in front until nearing home.

George Still was on the limit mark, while Arthur Penny was virtual scratch with 10 yards. George kept in front for several laps but the field gradually overhauled him and with a lap to go things looked very interesting.

Our old friend, George Still, started first, the last to start was Arthur Penny, who, although not on the scratch mark, gave proof of his fitness by clocking 15 mins. 5 secs. to record the fastest time.
It was also good to see George Still "still going strong" (no pun), and even at his time of life he managed to beat a few of the young' uns.

Good luck to them both; and a special word for George Still, who at 62 can cover ten miles at what seems to us a phenomenal pace—we expect him to win the race when he has had a little more experience!
In conclusion, I might add that much useful advice can be obtained from our old friend George Still, who was a first-class marathon runner during the early part of this century.

Still running! and has run in Veteran's sprint handicaps, and thereby been in the limelight in what few sporting columns we get in the press nowadays. George Still, no doubt, will be showing some of the lads around the common again—and leaving some of them behind!

George Still, our oldest competitive cross-country runner, who joined us in November, 1899, is indeed to be heartily congratulated on winning a prize in his 67th year in the Three Miles Road Handicap in October.

In second place was none other than George Still, who is 66, just 50 years older than the winner, and George is to be congratulated on his running and must be the envy of many who are years younger than he is.

There were 58 starters, which shows the popularity of the distance, which is perhaps a good omen. George Still gave us a performance of which many a younger man might be proud. The times suggest that it was a short course.

Sir Herbert Barker, the famous manipulative surgeon, who recently celebrated his 76th birthday, is said to owe his mental and physical alertness to his habit of taking a run, full out, for about a quarter of a mile, before breakfast. I wonder what Charlie Cook, George Still and Joe Deakin have got to say about that!

George Still has been one of the regulars at the Hall. George obviously doesn't mind the weather as he turned up on Boxing Day (remember how cold it was?) and gained second prize in the two miles run.

To George Still, our evergreen veteran, for taking the youngsters over the Common on a Saturday afternoon. To all those Officials who have given up their Saturday afternoons to assist as Judges at our Inter-Club and other meetings.

There was a large field for the 2 miles run and our "youngster," George Still, who is 68 years of age, was on the limit mark. Tom Carter was on the virtual scratch mark and he ran in really excellent style to work his way through the field to win a finely judged race.

Held on October 25th, and again a very large field turned out including our G.O.M. of the country, George Still. George is now turned 70 years of age yet each Saturday he can be seen running over the Common, and he usually takes along a school of junior runners with him.

It says much for our officials that this huge field was all despatched off their marks, with George Still, who is 71 years of age, on the limit mark, and then timed in at the finish to the satisfaction of all concerned.

Our G.O.M. of cross-country running, George Still, completed the course in good style, and is a wonder for his age of 71 years. George Still, who joined the club in 1899 was the first man away, followed by Jimmy Flatt and our past-president Bill Webb, but once they were caught they soon dropped to the rear of the field.
Included in the programme was a “Grandfathers” 100 yards race, put on by the Veterans' A.C., and among the runners was our own Dicky Best and George Still, who are still going strong.

George Still was first away as the limit man and he also finished the course in good style and it is really remarkable how George keeps going for year after year, seeing that he was in a " National " winning team in 1904.

One of the high-lights of the meeting, which attracted a good crowd, was the " Grandfathers " sprint over 100 yards, and the winner was none other than our old friend George Still now in his 74th year.

He was placed third in a race described as the 440 yards Club Championship. [Incidentally, at the same meeting, Harry Evans won the Mile Walk Handicap, off 10 yards; and Ted Good, present at our last A.G.M., won the Steeplechase Handicap, in which George Still (scratch) was third.
